newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Singapore Airlines seen eyeing Australia.
newsitem.headline: Singapore Airlines seen eyeing Australia.

text.p: Singapore Airlines Ltd (SIA) has positioned itself for a possible swoop on Australia's profitable domestic aviation market after teaming up with local airline Ansett on Friday, aviation analysts said.

SIA, one of the world's most profitable carriers, has the least to gain immediately from the international alliance signed on Friday morning with Ansett and Ansett's 50-percent shareholder, Air New Zealand, they told Reuters.
But SIA, with no domestic market of its own and facing an increasingly competitive global market, is said to see the real long-term value of the Ansett alliance as a way into Australia.
SIA chief executive Cheong Choong Kong told reporters on Friday that the airline had no immediate plans to operate in either the Australian or New Zealand domestic markets.
But he said SIA wanted more exposure to Australia's local airline market.
"This alliance actually gives us the confidence to expand further into Australia," Cheong said.
He denied the alliance was a strategic move to help it gain access to the tightly-regulated Australian market, but hinted that SIA wanted to see a more liberal market.
"It's not on the agenda of the alliance but if it helps to make 'open skies' a bit clearer, then we are all very happy about that," Cheong said.
Australia's domestic market was held tightly by Ansett and its arch rival, Qantas Airways Ltd.
Under the existing regulatory framework, the two airlines have a stranglehold on terminal space at domestic airports. An "open skies" policy would remove such barriers to entry.

"They (SIA) are very, very aware that growth is difficult for them and they need a domestic market and they are very keen on Australia," aviation analyst David Turner, of Shaw Stockbroking, told Reuters.
In Australia, revenue per passenger kilometre was almost double the average yield in the international market, Turner said.
Another analyst, who declined to be named, said SIA was keen to break into a domestic market.
"I think what SIA has been trying to do for quite a long period of time is to buy into somebody elses domestic market," the Hong Kong-based analyst said.
SIA was said by analysts to have conducted due diligence on Ansett in the early 1990s, but has so far been reluctant to buy into the airline, which is laden with debt.
Ansett plans to get its balance sheet and profitability into shape over the next three years.
Its two equal shareholders, Air New Zealand and media group News Corp Ltd, then plan to make a major offering of shares in the domestic airline and list it on Australia's share market.
Shaw's Turner predicted a float shortly before the 2000 Olympics, for which Ansett was the official domestic carrier.
Ansett's fledgling Asian operation, Ansett International, would remain a separate entity, he said.
Ansett International is only owned 49 percent by the parent Ansett Holdings Ltd. Two Australian institutions own the rest.
-- Mark Bendeich, Melbourne bureau 613-9286-1421
